pairs.t: Can a republic work in a large country?
pairs.q: Most writers before 1787 said a free republic had to be small. Would one government over thirteen states and a vast territory end in despotism?
pairs.f: A large republic is safer, not weaker. Representatives filter opinion, and a wide country holds so many interests that no single majority faction can take over. The national government has only listed powers; the states keep the rest.
pairs.a: One government cannot know or fairly govern so large and varied a country. Representatives would be few and distant, people would not trust them, and laws would need soldiers to enforce them. The plan would merge the states into one consolidated government.
pairs.after: The country grew from 13 states to 50. People still debate how much power belongs to the nation and how much to the states.

pairs.q: Was the country in such danger under the Articles of Confederation that it had to adopt the plan quickly?
pairs.f: Yes. Congress could not tax, pay its debts, regulate trade or enforce treaties; the country was near "the last stage of national humiliation." A government must act on individuals, not ask states for favors.
pairs.a: No. The country was at peace, the states were working, and the Articles needed amending, not replacing. Haste served men who wanted power; there was time to get it right.
pairs.after: Historians still discuss how serious the troubles of the 1780s were. Both sides agreed that the Confederation needed more power over trade and revenue.

pairs.t: Did the Convention go beyond its instructions?
pairs.q: The Convention was called to revise the Articles. It wrote a new constitution and said nine states, not all thirteen, could put it into effect.
pairs.f: The delegates were told to make the government adequate to the Union's needs; when the instructions conflicted, the purpose came first. In any case the plan was only a proposal, and the people, through ratifying conventions, would decide.
pairs.a: The delegates were sent to amend, not to replace. Writing "We, the people" instead of "We, the states" changed the nature of the Union without authority.
pairs.after: All thirteen states ratified by 1790, which settled the practical question; the legal argument is still discussed by historians.

pairs.t: The power to tax, and the "necessary and proper" clause
pairs.q: Should Congress have a general power to tax, and the power to make all laws "necessary and proper" to carry out its powers?
pairs.f: Money is the lifeblood of government; requisitions failed. Taxing power is shared with the states except on imports. The Necessary and Proper Clause only states what any grant of power implies, and laws beyond the Constitution are void.
pairs.a: Taxing power without limit, joined to the "sweeping" Necessary and Proper Clause and the Supremacy Clause, would let Congress take every source of revenue and leave the states nothing.
pairs.after: In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) the Supreme Court read "necessary and proper" broadly. The Sixteenth Amendment (1913) allowed a federal income tax without apportionment.

pairs.q: Should Congress be able to keep an army in peacetime and govern the militia?
pairs.f: Danger cannot be predicted, so defense powers cannot be capped. Congress, not the President, raises armies, and must vote their funding at least every two years. The states appoint militia officers, and the people are armed.
pairs.a: Peacetime armies have destroyed free governments throughout history. Congress's control of the militia could leave it neglected or turn it against the people. Armies should require a supermajority, and the militia should stay with the states.
pairs.after: The Second Amendment (1791) was one response. Its meaning is still debated in the courts and in public.

pairs.t: Is the House of Representatives large enough?
pairs.q: The first House had 65 members, about one for every 30,000 people at most. Could so few represent the people?
pairs.f: Very large assemblies become mobs. Representatives need to understand federal subjects, not every local detail. Electors are "not the rich, more than the poor," members must live under their own laws, and the House will grow with the census.
pairs.a: So few members would be wealthy, well-known men who cannot know the farmers and tradesmen they represent, and who could be bribed. A true representative body should be a likeness of the people.
pairs.after: The House grew with the population until it was fixed at 435 members by law in 1929 (it has had 435 since 1913, apart from a brief change after Alaska and Hawaii joined).

pairs.q: Article I lets Congress alter the states' rules for the times, places and manner of congressional elections.
pairs.f: Every government must be able to preserve itself; the states alone could refuse to hold elections and destroy the Union. The power covers only times, places and manner, not who may vote.
pairs.a: Congress could move polling places or set times to keep ordinary voters away and keep itself in power.
pairs.after: Congress later used the power to set a single federal Election Day and other rules. Disputes over election rules continue in Congress and the courts.

pairs.q: Senators chosen by state legislatures, two per state, for six years, sharing in treaties, appointments and impeachment trials.
pairs.f: Equal votes recognize the states' remaining sovereignty. A small, stable body brings wisdom and steadiness, guards against hasty laws, and protects the nation's reputation abroad.
pairs.a: Long terms with no rotation or recall would make senators permanent, an aristocracy joined to the President in executive business. Equal votes are unfair to large states.
pairs.after: The Seventeenth Amendment (1913) moved the choice of senators from state legislatures to the voters.

pairs.q: A single President, chosen by electors for four years, re-eligible without limit, commanding the military, with a veto and the pardon power.
pairs.f: "Energy in the Executive is a leading character in the definition of good government." One person acts with decision and can be held responsible. The President is elected, can be impeached, and shares treaties and appointments with the Senate; he is far from a king.
pairs.a: The office "squints towards monarchy." Without a council or a term limit, a President could build a court of followers, use the army, shield accomplices with pardons, and stay in office for life.
pairs.after: Washington's choice to serve two terms became custom; the Twenty-second Amendment (1951) made it law. The Twelfth Amendment (1804) changed how electors vote. Debates about the reach of presidential power continue.

pairs.t: The federal courts and judicial review
pairs.q: Judges serving during good behavior, with power over all cases arising under the Constitution and federal law, and a Supreme Court with final say.
pairs.f: The judiciary is "the least dangerous" branch, with neither force nor will. Courts must treat the Constitution as higher law and declare contrary acts void; this puts the people's will above both legislature and courts. Congress can impeach judges who overreach.
pairs.a: Judges serving for life, interpreting the Constitution by its "spirit," answerable to no one, would steadily expand federal power and swallow the state courts. Appeals on facts would weaken juries.
pairs.after: Marbury v. Madison (1803) established judicial review in practice. The Eleventh Amendment (1795) barred certain suits against states. Scholars and citizens still debate how far judicial power should reach.

pairs.t: Trial by jury in civil cases
pairs.q: The Constitution guaranteed juries in criminal trials but said nothing about civil cases.
pairs.f: Silence does not abolish civil juries; Congress can provide them. The states' practices differed too much for one rule.
pairs.a: Leaving civil juries out, and allowing appeals "as to law and fact," endangered one of the oldest protections of ordinary people.
pairs.after: The Seventh Amendment (1791) guaranteed jury trial in federal civil suits at common law over twenty dollars.

pairs.q: Should the Constitution include a list of the people's rights?
pairs.f: The Constitution grants only listed powers, so "why declare that things shall not be done which there is no power to do?" A list could be read to imply other powers. The Constitution already protects several rights, and is itself a bill of rights.
pairs.a: Because federal laws are supreme, state bills of rights would not protect people against the national government. Rights left to inference are lost; they must be written down: conscience, press, juries, searches, and more.
pairs.after: Several states ratified with recommended amendments. Madison proposed amendments in the First Congress, and the Bill of Rights was ratified in 1791. The Ninth Amendment speaks to Hamilton's worry about implied powers.

pairs.q: Both sides came to agree the plan had flaws. Should it be amended before ratification or after?
pairs.f: Amending first would need a new convention and new compromises among thirteen states. After adoption, amendments can be made one at a time. "I never expect to see a perfect work from imperfect man."
pairs.a: Once in power, the new government would have no reason to limit itself. "Why not amend, and then adopt it?"
pairs.after: The states adopted first and recommended amendments. Ten amendments were ratified by 1791, though many structural changes the Anti-Federalists wanted were not made.

pairs.q: The Constitution counted three-fifths of enslaved people for representation and direct taxes, protected the import trade in enslaved people until 1808, and required the return of people escaping slavery. Its text never uses the word "slave."
pairs.f: Federalist 42 calls the 1808 date a gain, since Congress could then end the import trade; Federalist 54 explains the three-fifths rule by voicing the argument of a Southern advocate, while calling parts of it "a little strained."
pairs.a: Anti-Federalists were divided. Mason objected to protecting the slave trade; others objected to counting enslaved people for representation; some Southern opponents feared the national government would one day act against slavery.
pairs.after: Congress banned the import trade effective 1808. Slavery was abolished by the Thirteenth Amendment (1865), and the three-fifths rule was replaced by the Fourteenth Amendment (1868).
